scenes.title:
Where are
all the drivers?
scenes.detail:
A crowd leaves. Ride requests spike.
The map needs fresh driver counts.
phrases: A stadium empties. Thousands of people request a ride.
How can a map show where drivers are right now?

scenes.title:
Divide the city.
Bucket locations.
scenes.detail:
Location -> cell ID
One driver belongs to one current cell.
phrases: Divide the city into small cells.
Map each driver's location to a cell identifier.

scenes.title:
Update state.
Don't recount.
scenes.detail:
Driver updates -> stream -> workers
Kafka is one possible stream technology.
phrases: Send location updates through a stream, such as Kafka.
Workers update state instead of recounting every driver.

scenes.title:
Leave one cell.
Enter another.
scenes.detail:
Keep driver -> latest cell.
Atomically decrement old and increment new.
phrases: Keep each driver's latest cell, plus a count per cell.
Cross a boundary: subtract from one cell, add to the other.

scenes.title:
Three updates.
Still one driver.
scenes.detail:
Same cell: refresh freshness, not the count.
Reject duplicate or older sequence numbers.
phrases: But count drivers, not messages.
Repeated updates in the same cell must not add another driver.

scenes.title:
No updates?
Expire stale state.
scenes.detail:
Illustrative 30-second timeout.
A worker removes state and decrements the count.
phrases: If updates stop, the driver might be offline.
An expiry worker removes stale state and adjusts the count.

scenes.title:
Read the summary.
Paint the map.
scenes.detail:
Colour = active driver count, not demand.
A maintained summary avoids a full recount.
phrases: Colour each cell by its count.
Read this small summary instead of every driver's location.

scenes.title:
A geographic
indexing grid.
scenes.detail:
Uber open-sourced H3.
Our diagram is illustrative, not actual H3 cells.
phrases: Uber's open-source H three provides a geographic grid.
These are illustrative hexagons, not real H three cells.

scenes.title:
Partition work.
Keep updates safe.
scenes.detail:
Within each region: atomic state + count changes.
Cross-region handoff is a separate concern.
phrases: Partition the workload by region as it grows.
Keep state and counter changes atomic within each region.

scenes.title:
What if updates
arrive late?
scenes.detail:
Comment your ordering strategy.
Surge pricing also needs a separate demand signal.
phrases: Driver count alone does not determine surge pricing.
How would you reject an older location update?

upload.title: How Driver Heatmaps Work | Uber-Style System Design | InterviewReel
upload.description:
Build an illustrative live driver heatmap: location-to-cell mapping, streamed updates, per-driver state and per-cell counts, movement, repeated messages, stale-driver expiry and regional partitioning.

This is a simplified interview design, NOT a claim about Uber's current internal architecture. Kafka is an example technology, not an assertion about Uber's stack. The animation uses a small planar hex grid, not actual H3 coordinates. The 30-second freshness timeout is illustrative.

Uber documents H3's role in geographic bucketing, marketplace analysis, pricing and dispatch: https://www.uber.com/blog/h3/
H3 documentation: https://h3geo.org/docs/

Correctness notes: state and counter changes must be atomic within their ownership boundary; stale expiry tasks must not remove fresher state. Cross-region handoff, failures and reconciliation require additional design. A cache TTL alone does not decrement an aggregate counter. Driver supply alone does not determine surge pricing: demand is a separate input.

Your turn: how would you handle duplicate and out-of-order location updates?

Original visuals and script with AI-generated narration. Like, subscribe and comment your approach.
